stories.title: What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow
stories.summary: President Donald Trump said John Ratcliffe's trip to Russia was a "semi-routine" visit but there is nothing routine about the CIA chief making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow. Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials on Tuesday - notably his opposite number in Russia's overseas spy agency, Sergei Naryshkin - after arriving unannounced on a US military plane, the Kremlin confirmed. It's been nearly five years since his predecessor William Burns made this trip and that was at a similarly tense time, just as Russia was drawing up plans to invade Ukraine. So, this is probably serious. In the absence of any official US comment on the reason for the mission, it is being widely reported Ratcliffe's trip was to warn Moscow not to escalate in relation to the stalemate in Ukraine - possibly by taking action against Nato members. One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states". The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles. And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said. News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally. But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock. Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.

stories.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
stories.summary: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said. Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used. It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school. One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported. The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported. Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide". "The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger. "I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said. State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence". The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday. Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come.

stories.title: Google, Microsoft and OpenAI among 100 firms calling for better cyber defences
stories.summary: A group of 100 firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, have signed an open letter calling on countries and organisations around the world to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them. The letter warns, external cyber-attacks which use AI will become both more widespread and more sophisticated in a matter of months as the technology rapidly improves. The group says current "status quo" security measures "won't be enough" and criticises the "historic under-resourcing" of security around critical infrastructure. "We have a limited window to improve cyber defences," the letter begins. Other firms to have signed the letter include banks such as Capital. One, payment processors MasterCard and Visa, and other major tech firms including Adobe, Oracle and IBM. They call on governments to provide "capable, defensive AI" and testing to hospitals and water utilities. But it is also true that many of the most powerful AI have been developed by some of these companies - and they are not all easily available. Mythos, developed by Anthropic, was said by the firm to be able to find weaknesses in systems in seconds which have long evaded human hackers. It found one in a legacy platform which had remained undiscovered for 27 years. Anthropic has restricted access to Mythos on the grounds that it is too powerful to fall into the wrong hands. Meanwhile, a group of AI agents being tested by OpenAI in July were able to set up secret message boards to communicate with each other and work together, resulting in a successful attack on a rival company, Hugging Face - which has also signed the letter.

stories.title: Foreign ministers to hold meeting on Iran in Istanbul on Sunday — media
stories.summary: The ministers will discuss ways to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the regional security situation
article_sentences: BERLIN, August 27.
Foreign ministers from Britain, Germany, France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey will meet in Istanbul on August 30 to talk about Iran, DPA reported, citing German government sources.
Germany and Turkey initiated the talks.
The ministers will discuss ways to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the regional security situation.
The participating countries expect the meeting to send a signal to the United States that talks with Iran should continue.
The agenda will also include the situation in the Black Sea and Ukrainian grain exports, the news agency reported.
